subject: Nvidia guides to $130B and assumes zero from China
bodyMarkdown:
Nvidia reported its biggest quarter ever after the close last night, two days after Washington made it harder to sell the chips that produced it. If you hold an S&P 500 index fund in a TFSA or an RRSP, you own a piece of that collision, because Nvidia is roughly 6 per cent of the index, second only to Apple.

## What Nvidia actually reported

Revenue came in at $115.8 billion for the quarter, up 103 per cent from a year ago and up 20 per cent from the previous three months. Data centre alone was $107.6 billion. Adjusted earnings were $2.68 a share against the $2.47 analysts had pencilled in, on revenue they had pegged near $108.8 billion. For the current quarter the company guided to $130 billion, plus or minus 3 per cent, against an average analyst estimate of $125.1 billion according to CNBC. Here is the line I keep rereading. That $130 billion assumes no data centre compute revenue from China at all, after $2.4 billion of Hopper chips shipped there last quarter. A company that can mark its China data centre business down to zero and still promise 12 per cent growth in a single quarter is saying something about demand everywhere else.

## Washington closed the cloud door

On Monday the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an **interim final rule**, meaning one that binds before the public comment window closes, titled Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors. It builds a new data centre control. You now need a licence to send advanced chips to any facility, anywhere on earth, that might give companies headquartered in China, Macau or other Country Group D:5 destinations access to more than 12 million aggregate **total processing performance**, which is Commerce's combined measure of chip speed and precision. TechTimes put that threshold at roughly 750 Nvidia H100s. Client alerts from Pillsbury and WilmerHale read the rule as reaching remote access rather than physical shipment alone, and confirm it formally rescinds the January 2025 AI Diffusion Rule. Chips bound for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil need licences now too. Canada is not on that list. Data centres already serving covered customers get 90 days to apply.

## The chair who is not Jensen Huang

Colette Kress hosted that call as interim chief executive, five days after Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 and the board handed her both jobs while it searches for a permanent replacement. CNN reported on Tuesday that the board has ruled out Huang's return, with the chair saying he has every confidence in Kress, after Huang said he would be honoured to come back if the board allowed it. Markets have been voting on the policy rather than the person. Monday's rule knocked Nvidia down about 4 per cent, pulled the chip index down more than 5 per cent, and left the S&P 500 at its lowest close since July by CNBC's account. The shares recovered after the numbers landed. The quarter answered the demand question. Nobody has answered who runs the world's most valuable chip company next year.

## The takeaway

The rule is scheduled to hit the Federal Register tomorrow, which starts a 60 day comment window and the 90 day clock for data centres already serving covered customers. I would not move a retirement account on one quarter, however good it looks. What I am watching is whether Nvidia still guides to zero from China when it reports again in February, because Monday's rule turns that assumption into something closer to permanent. If you want one clean read on whether the AI buildout is cooling, it is that $130 billion, and it is not cooling.
